ety.text: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”).

senses.d: Foreign, especially in an exciting way.
ex: Nothing was so splendid and exotic as the ambassador.
senses.zh: 有異國情調；外來的；異國的

senses.d: Being or relating to an option with features that make it more complex than commonly traded options.
Being or relating to various wagers, such as the trifecta, that involve betting on the finishing positions of multiple competitors across one or more races.
Denoting or relating to any animal that is not a cat or dog, requiring specialised healthcare
An organism that is exotic to an environment; an introduced species.
A person not native to a particular area; a foreigner.

ex: Glueballs, theoretical particles composed only of gluons, are exotics.

grp.label: foreign, with the connotation of excitingly foreign

ety.text: Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós)bor. Latin exōticuslbor. Portuguese exótico Learned borrowing from Latin exōticus.

Proto-Indo-European *sed-der. Proto-Indo-European *sodós? Proto-Hellenic *hodós Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós) Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos)der. Latin exodusder. English exodus From Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, procession, departure”). Doublet of exodos. From late Old English only as a proper noun, Exodus, the biblical book; use as a common noun is from the early 17th century.

senses.d: A sudden departure of a large number of people.
ex: At 18ʰ00′, 21 minutes before sunset, the migrants started to depart in waves as already described for other exodi; […]

senses.d: To depart from a place in a large group.

ety.text: From Late Latin exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos, “expedition, departure”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ὁδός (hodós, “path, road”).
